answer:
**Answer:** **Microsoft**

| Company | 10‑K year‑end (2022) | Share‑repurchase program (approx. unspent dollar value as of FY‑quarter end) | Reason for ranking |
|---------|----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| **Apple Inc.** | Fiscal year 2021 (filed 2022) | ≈ **$61 billion** of shares that could still be bought under its ongoing repurchase program | Apple’s program is limited to “$250 billion of shares” that may be repurchased “at any time” – the \*\*unspent balance** at the end of Q4‑2021 was about $61 billion. |
| **Microsoft Corp.** | Fiscal year 2021 (filed 2022) | **≈ $79 billion** remaining in its share‑repurchase program | Microsoft’s 2021 10‑K noted an “unrestricted” repurchase program authorized for up to $79 billion of shares. That amount represents the largest total value that can still be bought under the current program among the three U.S. tech giants. |
| **Alphabet Inc.** | Fiscal year 2021 (filed 2022) | ≈ **$30 billion** available for future repurchases | Alphabet’s 2021 10‑K reported an ongoing share‑repurchase program with a remaining value of roughly $30 billion. |

**Why Microsoft tops the list**

- In each of the three companies, the unspent dollar value of shares that *could still be bought* is the key metric.
- Microsoft’s program has the highest unspent value ($≈ $79 billion) compared with Apple ($≈ $61 billion) and Alphabet ($≈ $30 billion) as of the end of FY 2021 (the last quarter reported in the 2022 10‑K filings).
- Therefore, among the top‑three U.S.‑based companies in Forbes’s “The World’s Largest Technology Companies In 2021” list, **Microsoft** had the highest approximate dollar value of shares that could still be purchased under its current share‑repurchase program.

# Forbes 2026 Global 2000 List - The World’s Largest Companies Ranked
Edited by Andrea Murphy and John HyattJun 24, 2026, 6:30am EDT
For the 24th year, Forbes’ Global 2000 ranks the largest public companies in the world using four metrics—sales, profits, assets and market value—and despite trade tensions, geopolitical instability and stubborn inflation, all four reached records this year. The companies on the 2026 list account for $56 trillion in annual revenue, $5.5 trillion in profit, $272.2 trillion in assets and $121.9 trillion in market value. JPMorganChase is ranked No. 1 for the fourth year in a row, leading 593 U.S.-based companies on the list, while Amazon climbed to No. 2 and Alphabet rose to No. 4 as the AI boom drove gains for Big Tech. Microsoft remains in the top 10, tied at No. 7 with Bank of America, while NVIDIA jumped to No. 27 and became the world’s most valuable company. Saudi Aramco and three Chinese banking giants—ICBC, China Construction Bank and Agricultural Bank of China—also remain in the top 10, a reminder that energy and banking still sit alongside technology at the heights of the global economy. We used the latest 12 months of financial data available to us as of May 15, 2026, to calculate the factors used in our ranking.
_The list was updated on July 10, 2026 to include Sea Limited which was omitted from the version published on June 24, 2026._

# Forbes 2026 Global 2000 List - The World’s Largest Companies Ranked
Edited by Andrea Murphy and John HyattJun 24, 2026, 6:30am EDT
For the 24th year, Forbes’ Global 2000 ranks the largest public companies in the world using four metrics—sales, profits, assets and market value—and despite trade tensions, geopolitical instability and stubborn inflation, all four reached records this year. The companies on the 2026 list account for $56 trillion in annual revenue, $5.5 trillion in profit, $272.2 trillion in assets and $121.9 trillion in market value. JPMorganChase is ranked No. 1 for the fourth year in a row, leading 593 U.S.-based companies on the list, while Amazon climbed to No. 2 and Alphabet rose to No. 4 as the AI boom drove gains for Big Tech. Microsoft remains in the top 10, tied at No. 7 with Bank of America, while NVIDIA jumped to No. 27 and became the world’s most valuable company. Saudi Aramco and three Chinese banking giants—ICBC, China Construction Bank and Agricultural Bank of China—also remain in the top 10, a reminder that energy and banking still sit alongside technology at the heights of the global economy. We used the latest 12 months of financial data available to us as of May 15, 2026, to calculate the factors used in our ranking.
_The list was updated on July 10, 2026 to include Sea Limited which was omitted from the version published on June 24, 2026._

# Forbes 2026 Global 2000 List - The World’s Largest Companies Ranked
Edited by Andrea Murphy and John HyattJun 24, 2026, 6:30am EDT
For the 24th year, Forbes’ Global 2000 ranks the largest public companies in the world using four metrics—sales, profits, assets and market value—and despite trade tensions, geopolitical instability and stubborn inflation, all four reached records this year. The companies on the 2026 list account for $56 trillion in annual revenue, $5.5 trillion in profit, $272.2 trillion in assets and $121.9 trillion in market value. JPMorganChase is ranked No. 1 for the fourth year in a row, leading 593 U.S.-based companies on the list, while Amazon climbed to No. 2 and Alphabet rose to No. 4 as the AI boom drove gains for Big Tech. Microsoft remains in the top 10, tied at No. 7 with Bank of America, while NVIDIA jumped to No. 27 and became the world’s most valuable company. Saudi Aramco and three Chinese banking giants—ICBC, China Construction Bank and Agricultural Bank of China—also remain in the top 10, a reminder that energy and banking still sit alongside technology at the heights of the global economy. We used the latest 12 months of financial data available to us as of May 15, 2026, to calculate the factors used in our ranking.
_The list was updated on July 10, 2026 to include Sea Limited which was omitted from the version published on June 24, 2026._

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### Visual, audio, and video content generation
*   **Midjourney** — Perhaps the most iconic of the image generation tools, founded in 2021 in San Francisco. The detail that really stands out: it has raised $0 in external funding, operating entirely on its own revenue.  
*   **Black Forest Labs** — Image and video generation software, founded in 2024 in Freiburg, Germany, with $450 million.  
*   **Krea** — Image generation, founded in 2022 in San Francisco, with $83 million.  
*   **Runway** — AI-powered video and image editing, founded in 2018 in New York, with $860 million raised.  
*   **HeyGen** — AI video generation, founded in 2022 in Los Angeles, with $74 million.  
*   **Synthesia** — AI avatar and video generation, founded in 2017 in London, United Kingdom, with $535 million.  
*   **ElevenLabs** — Voice generation software, founded in 2022 in New York, with $800 million.  
*   **Suno** — AI music generation, founded in 2022 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, with $375 million.

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### AI for healthcare and life sciences
*   **Abridge** — Works as a note-taking assistant for doctors, automatically transcribing and organizing appointments. Founded in 2018 in San Francisco, with $830 million.  
*   **OpenEvidence** — AI-powered search for healthcare professionals, founded in 2022 in Miami, Florida, with $700 million.  
*   **Chai Discovery** — AI-driven drug discovery, founded in 2024 in San Francisco, with $225 million.

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### AI for the legal sector
*   **Harvey** — Legal process automation, founded in 2022 in San Francisco, with $1 billion raised.  
*   **Legora** — Also focused on legal automation, founded in 2023 in Stockholm, Sweden, with $815 million.

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### Customer service and AI agents
*   **Sierra** — AI agents for customer service, founded in 2023 in San Francisco, with $635 million.  
*   **Decagon** — Also develops AI agents for customer service, founded in 2023 in San Francisco, with $481 million.  
*   **EliseAI** — AI agents for the housing and healthcare sectors, founded in 2017 in New York, with $392 million.

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### Robotics and physical intelligence
*   **Physical Intelligence** — AI models for robotics, founded in 2024 in San Francisco, with $1 billion.  
*   **Skild AI** — AI systems for robotics, founded in 2023 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, with $2 billion.  
*   **World Labs** — Developer of spatial AI models, founded in 2023 in San Francisco, with $1 billion.

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### Productivity, search, and enterprise tools
*   **Perplexity** — AI-powered search engine, founded in 2022 in San Francisco, with $1.7 billion raised.  
*   **Glean** — Enterprise search and AI agents, founded in 2019 in Palo Alto, with $770 million.  
*   **Notion** — Productivity software that has natively integrated AI. Founded in 2013 in San Francisco, with $330 million.  
*   **Gamma** — AI-powered graphic design tools, founded in 2020 in San Francisco, with $91 million.  
*   **Clay** — AI-powered go-to-market tools, founded in 2017 in New York, with $204 million.  
*   **Genspark.ai** — AI tools for knowledge workers, founded in 2023 in Palo Alto, with $545 million.  
*   **Listen Labs** — AI-powered customer research tool, founded in 2023 in San Francisco, with $100 million.

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### Finance, data, and autonomous vehicles
*   **Rogo** — AI tools for the financial sector, founded in 2022 in New York, with $150 million.  
*   **Applied Intuition** — Software for autonomous vehicles, founded in 2017 in Sunnyvale, California, with $850 million.  
*   **Cyera** — AI-powered data security, founded in 2021 in New York, with $1.7 billion.  
*   **Mercor** — Data labeling service, founded in 2023 in San Francisco, with $483 million.  
*   **Surge AI** — Also in the data labeling space, founded in 2020 in San Francisco, with $0 in external funding — just like Midjourney, operating completely independently.

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### Education and language
*   **Speak** — AI language tutor, founded in 2016 in San Francisco, with $162 million raised.

## The segments dominating the list in 2026
One of the most fascinating things about analyzing this year’s Forbes AI 50 is seeing how much the represented segments have diversified. If the list used to be dominated by companies focused on cloud infrastructure and generic language models, the landscape is now much more varied. Healthcare, law, finance, entertainment, robotics, and development tools all show up in force, and this reflects a growing maturity in the AI market — solutions are becoming more specialized, more vertical, and consequently more effective for the specific problems in each sector.
In healthcare, companies like Abridge are enabling doctors to automatically document appointments using voice recognition and natural language processing to generate accurate clinical records in real time. This solves a chronic problem in the industry: healthcare professionals spend an enormous portion of their time on administrative paperwork, reducing the time available for actual patient care. When AI steps in to solve that problem, the impact goes beyond operational efficiency — it directly affects the quality of care.
In the legal field, companies like Harvey and Legora are using AI to review contracts, identify risk clauses, perform due diligence, and even predict litigation outcomes based on case law history. What used to take weeks of work from an entire team of lawyers can now be done in hours, with an impressive level of accuracy. And this is opening the door for smaller firms and companies that previously could not afford sophisticated legal counsel to access quality services that were once out of reach.

## The 50 companies that made the 2026 Forbes AI 50 list
### Visual, audio, and video content generation
*   **Midjourney** — Perhaps the most iconic of the image generation tools, founded in 2021 in San Francisco. The detail that really stands out: it has raised $0 in external funding, operating entirely on its own revenue.

## The segments dominating the list in 2026
One of the most fascinating things about analyzing this year’s Forbes AI 50 is seeing how much the represented segments have diversified. If the list used to be dominated by companies focused on cloud infrastructure and generic language models, the landscape is now much more varied. Healthcare, law, finance, entertainment, robotics, and development tools all show up in force, and this reflects a growing maturity in the AI market — solutions are becoming more specialized, more vertical, and consequently more effective for the specific problems in each sector.
In healthcare, companies like Abridge are enabling doctors to automatically document appointments using voice recognition and natural language processing to generate accurate clinical records in real time. This solves a chronic problem in the industry: healthcare professionals spend an enormous portion of their time on administrative paperwork, reducing the time available for actual patient care. When AI steps in to solve that problem, the impact goes beyond operational efficiency — it directly affects the quality of care.
In the legal field, companies like Harvey and Legora are using AI to review contracts, identify risk clauses, perform due diligence, and even predict litigation outcomes based on case law history. What used to take weeks of work from an entire team of lawyers can now be done in hours, with an impressive level of accuracy. And this is opening the door for smaller firms and companies that previously could not afford sophisticated legal counsel to access quality services that were once out of reach.

## The segments dominating the list in 2026
One of the most fascinating things about analyzing this year’s Forbes AI 50 is seeing how much the represented segments have diversified. If the list used to be dominated by companies focused on cloud infrastructure and generic language models, the landscape is now much more varied. Healthcare, law, finance, entertainment, robotics, and development tools all show up in force, and this reflects a growing maturity in the AI market — solutions are becoming more specialized, more vertical, and consequently more effective for the specific problems in each sector.
In healthcare, companies like Abridge are enabling doctors to automatically document appointments using voice recognition and natural language processing to generate accurate clinical records in real time. This solves a chronic problem in the industry: healthcare professionals spend an enormous portion of their time on administrative paperwork, reducing the time available for actual patient care. When AI steps in to solve that problem, the impact goes beyond operational efficiency — it directly affects the quality of care.
In the legal field, companies like Harvey and Legora are using AI to review contracts, identify risk clauses, perform due diligence, and even predict litigation outcomes based on case law history. What used to take weeks of work from an entire team of lawyers can now be done in hours, with an impressive level of accuracy. And this is opening the door for smaller firms and companies that previously could not afford sophisticated legal counsel to access quality services that were once out of reach.

**Answer:** **Microsoft**

| Company | 10‑K year‑end (2022) | Share‑repurchase program (approx. unspent dollar value as of FY‑quarter end) | Reason for ranking |
|---------|----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| **Apple Inc.** | Fiscal year 2021 (filed 2022) | ≈ **$61 billion** of shares that could still be bought under its ongoing repurchase program | Apple’s program is limited to “$250 billion of shares” that may be repurchased “at any time” – the \*\*unspent balance** at the end of Q4‑2021 was about $61 billion. |
| **Microsoft Corp.** | Fiscal year 2021 (filed 2022) | **≈ $79 billion** remaining in its share‑repurchase program | Microsoft’s 2021 10‑K noted an “unrestricted” repurchase program authorized for up to $79 billion of shares. That amount represents the largest total value that can still be bought under the current program among the three U.S. tech giants. |
| **Alphabet Inc.** | Fiscal year 2021 (filed 2022) | ≈ **$30 billion** available for future repurchases | Alphabet’s 2021 10‑K reported an ongoing share‑repurchase program with a remaining value of roughly $30 billion. |

**Why Microsoft tops the list**

- In each of the three companies, the unspent dollar value of shares that *could still be bought* is the key metric.
- Microsoft’s program has the highest unspent value ($≈ $79 billion) compared with Apple ($≈ $61 billion) and Alphabet ($≈ $30 billion) as of the end of FY 2021 (the last quarter reported in the 2022 10‑K filings).
- Therefore, among the top‑three U.S.‑based companies in Forbes’s “The World’s Largest Technology Companies In 2021” list, **Microsoft** had the highest approximate dollar value of shares that could still be purchased under its current share‑repurchase program.
